title: Authentication at Scale
description: Master OAuth 2.0, OIDC, token lifecycle management, refresh token theft detection, and enterprise SSO patterns used by companies processing billions of auth requests daily.

segments.text: Authentication seems simple until you're handling a billion logins per day across mobile, web, and API clients. OAuth 2.0 isn't an authentication protocol — it's an authorization framework. This distinction trips up even senior engineers and creates real security vulnerabilities when misunderstood.

The authorization code flow with PKCE is the gold standard for all clients — web, mobile, and single-page apps. The client generates a random code verifier, hashes it into a code challenge, sends the challenge to the auth server. On callback, the client sends the original verifier. No client secret ever touches the browser.

OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on top of OAuth. The ID token is a JWT containing who the user is — sub claim, email, name. The access token controls what they can do. Never use the access token for identity. Google's OIDC implementation handles over ten billion token validations per day across all Google services.

Access tokens should be short-lived — fifteen minutes maximum. Refresh tokens last longer — days or weeks — and are used to get new access tokens. This limits the blast radius of a stolen access token. If an attacker steals one, it's useless in fifteen minutes.

Refresh token theft detection is critical. Use rotation — every time a refresh token is used, issue a new one and invalidate the old. If the old token is used again, someone stole it. Immediately revoke the entire token family. Auth0 and Okta implement this pattern, catching token replay attacks in real time.
A user's refresh token is stolen from their mobile device. The attacker uses it before the legitimate user does. Now both have valid refresh tokens. How does your system detect and handle this?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you detect that a refresh token has been stolen and is being used by two parties simultaneously?

segments.text: Enterprise SSO with SAML enables one login for all corporate applications. The identity provider — Okta, Azure AD — holds credentials. Service providers redirect users to the IdP, which returns a signed SAML assertion. The service provider trusts the assertion because it can verify the IdP's signature.

Multi-factor authentication: something you know plus something you have. TOTP — time-based one-time passwords like Google Authenticator — are widely used but phishable. WebAuthn with hardware keys like YubiKey is phishing-resistant because the authentication is bound to the origin domain. Google eliminated all phishing attacks internally by requiring hardware keys.

At scale, token validation must be fast. JWT validation is stateless — verify the signature locally without hitting the auth server. But revocation becomes the problem. You can't revoke a JWT before expiry without a blocklist. The solution: short-lived access tokens plus a distributed token blocklist cached in Redis with TTL matching token expiry.
You're designing auth for a system with fifty million users, mobile and web clients, and enterprise SSO requirements. What token strategy, storage, and MFA approach would you choose?
segments.thought_prompt: Design an auth system for 50M users supporting mobile, web, and enterprise SSO. What are your key decisions?

segments.text: Authentication at scale requires layered defenses: OAuth 2.0 with PKCE for all clients, short-lived JWTs with refresh token rotation, OIDC for identity, SAML for enterprise SSO, and WebAuthn for phishing-resistant MFA. The Staff-level insight: auth is the one system where a single bug can compromise everything. Design for defense in depth.
